when: Markets, street stalls and small shops — anywhere there is no printed price tag.
It is also how a negotiation starts: asking the price is not a commitment to buy.

variants.note: Point at the item while you say it.
The one to know in fruit and vegetable markets, where everything is priced per 斤 rather than per item.

mistakes: Say duōshao, not duōshǎo — 少 loses its third tone inside this word.
In supermarkets and chain stores the price is printed on the shelf. This question belongs where prices are actually negotiated, not everywhere you buy something.

when: When pointing is doing most of the work — a menu, a display case, a market stall, or a photo on your phone.
Say it with your finger already on the item, because 这个 is only as precise as the thing you are touching; said without pointing it turns into 哪个？

variants.note: 要 takes a number plus a measure word directly: 两个, 三碗, 四张. The measure word is never optional.
就 narrows the choice. It is the answer for when somebody is offering you something and you want the offering to stop.
A two-word order plus 谢谢 is entirely normal at a counter. Chinese gets shorter under pressure, not more formal.

mistakes: 给我 is not the polite 'give me' of English. On its own it is an instruction, which is why 我要这个 is the safer default and 给我 is kept for people you know.
要 is want-in-order-to-receive and 想 is want-as-a-feeling. 我想要这个 sounds hesitant and can read as 'I would quite like this', so use 要 when you are actually ordering.
There is no word for 'the'. 这个 is doing that job — it means the one you mean — so the English habit of naming an item without pointing at it gets you 哪个？ in return.

when: Say it as you order rather than when the food arrives — chilli usually goes into the wok, so a dish that reaches you mild had to be cooked that way from the start.
It is worth saying even if you like heat, because 辣 in Sichuan and Hunan cooking is a baseline rather than a flavour, and 不要辣 is understood everywhere without further explanation.

variants.note: 放 (to put in) turns the wish into an instruction, which is what you want when the order is being written down rather than remembered.
Two syllables and it fits on a menu line. 微 is the 微 of 微信 (WeChat), meaning tiny, so 微辣 is the lowest setting that still counts as spicy.
Stronger than 不要辣: it makes chilli something you cannot have rather than something you would rather skip this time, and waiters remember it.

mistakes: 不要辣 keeps the 要 (to want), so it is literally "don't want spicy". A bare 不辣 sounds like a claim about the dish instead of a request about your order, which is not what a waiter is listening for.
辣 covers chilli heat only. The numbing buzz of Sichuan peppercorn is a separate word — 麻 (má) — so a dish can be 不辣 and still leave your mouth tingling.
Some dishes are chilli-free before you ask. 白灼 (blanched), 清蒸 (steamed) and 清汤 (clear soup) have no chilli in the recipe, so ordering one of those is simpler than negotiating.

when: Use it the moment you sit down, or at the door when you cannot see a single menu on any table.
In many restaurants the menu is not on paper at all — you order by scanning a QR code on the table, so if the answer is a pointed finger at a code, that is normal, not a refusal.

variants.note: The same request as a direct ask — 有…吗 asks whether it exists, 给… asks for it straight out. Either works; this one is shorter.

variants.en: Do you have an English menu?
variants.note: Many restaurants keep a second menu just for visitors, but it is often kept behind the counter — you have to ask for it.

variants.en: Do you have a menu with pictures?
variants.note: A picture menu solves ordering even with zero Chinese — pointing works, and the photos also show you the real portion size.

mistakes: 菜单 (càidān) is the physical menu; 点菜 (diǎncài) is the act of ordering. 有菜单吗 asks for the booklet — when you are ready to order, the word is 点菜 or 我要点菜.
In QR-code restaurants there may be no paper menu anywhere, so 有菜单吗 can earn a puzzled look. The question that always works is 扫码点菜吗？ (do I order by scanning the code?)
Small eateries often paint the menu on the wall behind the counter. Staff will answer 有 with a nod and a pointed finger — look up before you conclude they have no menu.

replies.py: Sǎo zhuō shàng de mǎ jiù xíng.
replies.en: Just scan the code on the table.
There is only the Chinese one.

when: Said while eating, about the food in front of you — to the cook, your host, or whoever chose the restaurant.
Also works before you taste it, when a dish arrives and looks or smells good.

variants.note: The version you will hear most at the table.
Calmer than 好吃 — for when you want to sound a little less effusive.

mistakes: Do not use it for drinks — that is 好喝 (hǎohē).
Compliment the specific dish, not 'the food' in general. 好吃 is about what is in your mouth right now.

when: Say it while ordering or when a host is putting food on your plate, and it rules out meat in one sentence without naming every animal.
肉 covers pork, beef and lamb all at once, so the sentence stays short even when your reason — diet, religion or taste — is a long story.

variants.note: Pork is the default meat in Chinese cooking, so this one word unblocks most menus.

variants.en: Chicken is fine, but no beef.
variants.note: Carve exceptions in one breath with 可以…不吃 — no need for a second sentence.

variants.en: Not a bit of meat at all.
variants.note: 一点…都 makes it emphatic — stronger than a plain 不吃 when you want no meat anywhere.

mistakes: Meat hides in the stock as well as on the plate — soup, congee and even vegetable stir-fries are often cooked with pork broth, so ask 汤里有肉吗？ about anything liquid.
肉 by itself defaults to pork in dish names: 鱼香肉丝 contains no fish — it is shredded pork in a fish-fragrant sauce, one of the most famous dishes in China.
不吃 is heard as a preference, and the kitchen may try to talk you out of it. If it is a hard rule — medical or religious — switch to 不能吃, which sounds like a law rather than a wish.

replies.en: There is no meat in this dish.

replies.py: Nà gěi nín shàng qīngcài ba?
replies.en: Then how about we bring you greens?

when: Say it once the order is in but no drinks have arrived — in most Chinese restaurants water is not poured automatically, it has to be asked for.
It is also the phrase to fall back on when a shared pot of tea is going round the table and you would rather have plain water for yourself.

variants.en: I'd like a glass of water.
variants.note: 一杯 is one glass; swap in 瓶 (bīng) for a bottle.
Using 来 as a request is very common at the table — short and still polite.
Asking for 热 on purpose is normal, because that is what most places serve.

mistakes: Do not expect cold water. What arrives is 热水 (hot) or 温水 (warm), and ordering 冰水 in winter can get you a genuinely puzzled look.
不要水 is a refusal, not a request. 我不要水 means "I don't want any water" — the verb you need here is 要 or 给.
水 on its own means drinking water rather than the bottled kind. For a sealed bottle ask for 矿泉水 (kuàngquánshuǐ), and for sparkling you will usually have to name a brand.

when: Say it when the meal is over and there is food left. Doggy bags are normal in most Chinese restaurants, and asking for one is not seen as an imposition.

It is worth knowing the three words that are not interchangeable here: 打包 is boxing up what you did not finish, 带走 is taking a fresh order away, and 外卖 is delivery. A waiter acts on whichever one you use.

variants.en: Could you box this up for me, please.
variants.note: 麻烦 (sorry to trouble you) plus 帮我 (help me) is the standard polite frame for asking staff to do something: 麻烦帮我拿一下 (pass me that, please) is built the same way.

variants.en: I can't finish it — box it up.
variants.note: Gives the reason and the instruction in one breath. Chinese pairs the two often, and it saves a round of questions.

variants.en: Do you have a box for this?
variants.note: The version to use when the food is still on the table and no waiter is nearby. 盒 is the box itself — 饭盒 (lunch box) is built the same way.

mistakes: Doggy bags carry no stigma in China. Not finishing a dish is ordinary, and asking for a box reads as liking the food enough to want it again later.
打包 is the word that gets action for leftovers. 带走 is a request about how an order leaves, so it fits a fresh order better than a half-eaten plate.
Say it before you pay. The box comes from the kitchen or the front desk, and asking at the counter afterwards means a second trip.

replies.py: Hézi yào jiā yí kuài qián.
replies.en: The box is one yuan extra.

when: In markets, street stalls and shops where the price was spoken to you rather than printed on a tag.
It opens a negotiation rather than ending one: in China this is the first move in bargaining, and it is normally said with a smile.

variants.note: The sentence that follows this one. On its own it is a request; after 太贵了 it becomes an offer to keep talking.

variants.en: That is a bit expensive, isn't it?
variants.note: The 吧 turns a verdict into a shared observation, which is much easier for a seller to answer.
The polite version. 可以…吗 is the frame for asking permission, so it lands softly even in a loud market.

mistakes: On its own it can sound like a flat refusal. The bargaining happens in the next sentence, so follow it with 便宜一点 or 可以便宜点吗 instead of repeating it.
It is about a price someone quoted you, not a price on a menu. In a supermarket or a chain restaurant the price is fixed and the phrase has no answer.
Keep the tone light. A hard 太贵了 aimed at a shopkeeper reads as an insult to the goods; the same words said cheerfully are an invitation to bargain.

replies.py: Yǐjīng shì zuì dī jià le.
replies.en: That is already the lowest price.

when: At the end of a meal in a sit-down restaurant: catch a server's eye and say it, or say it at the till on your way out.
The bill covers the whole table, and one person settling it is the norm, so it is also the phrase you use when you intend to pay for everyone.

variants.note: The standard word in Taiwan and much of the south. Understood everywhere on the mainland, so either one works.
Said while reaching for your phone. In China everyone offers at once, so saying it first is polite rather than pushy.
Ask before the cashier starts, because the default assumption is one payment for the table.

mistakes: 买单 is the mainland phrase and 结账 is what people say in Taiwan. Both are understood, but 结账 in a Beijing restaurant sounds slightly unusual.
Tipping is not expected and a service charge would be printed on the menu, so the number on the bill is the number you pay.
If you need an official receipt for expenses, ask for 发票 (fāpiào) at the moment you pay. It has to be issued from the original transaction and cannot be added afterwards.

when: Any restaurant, station, shopping centre or hotel lobby.
Public toilets in China are common and almost always free — you rarely need to buy something first.

variants.note: The politer word. Use it in hotels, airports and nicer restaurants.
This is the word printed on most public signs.

variants.zh: 可以借用一下洗手间吗？
variants.note: Needed in small shops and private businesses where the toilet is not public.

mistakes: Ask about the room, not about yourself — do not translate 'I need to go to the bathroom' word for word.
哪里 (nǎlǐ) and 哪儿 (nǎr) are the same question word. The second carries an r-coloured ending and sounds more Beijing; both are understood everywhere.

when: Ask it of a passer-by, a hotel front desk or a taxi driver when you know the station is nearby but not which direction it lies in.
It is also the phrase for the moment a long-distance bus drops you somewhere unfamiliar and you need to work out how to continue by rail.

variants.en: How do I get to the train station?
variants.note: 怎么走 asks for the route rather than the location, which is often more useful.

variants.zh: 打扰一下，火车站在哪儿？
variants.en: Sorry to bother you, where is the train station?
variants.note: 打扰一下 is the standard opener with a stranger, and it buys you patience.
Use it when you can already see a big building and just want it confirmed.

mistakes: 火车 is the train, not the station. 车站 on its own means any station — bus, coach or rail — so 火车 alone will not get you to a ticket hall.
在哪儿 asks where something is, while 怎么走 asks how to get there. The 哪儿 and 哪里 forms are the same word at different registers, so both are safe, but neither gives you a route.
Big cities have more than one, and drivers may not know which you mean. 高铁站 (gāotiězhàn) is the one for bullet trains and is often a completely different building.

replies.en: Turn left at the junction ahead.

when: When the conversation has to change shape right now — somebody is explaining something at speed and none of it is landing.

It is a statement rather than a request, so it works best as the first thing you say; coming in mid-sentence it sounds like you are giving up on what they just said, which is when 我中文说得不好 is the better choice.

variants.en: I only know a tiny bit of Chinese.
variants.note: 只会 is 'only know how to'. 一点点 is the modest conversational amount — smaller, and warmer, than 一点.

variants.py: Nǐ kěyǐ dǎzì gěi wǒ kàn.
variants.en: You could type it out for me.
variants.note: A phone keyboard crosses the gap faster than speech. 打字 is typing and 写 is writing by hand; the two are not interchangeable.

variants.py: Bù hǎoyìsi, wǒ bú tài huì.
variants.note: 不太会 says the skill is thin rather than absent. Both truer and easier on the other person than a flat 我不会.

mistakes: 不会 is about a skill you never picked up, and 不能 is about not being able to right now. Saying 我不说中文 instead reads as a choice you are making, which is why it lands as rude rather than apologetic.

This sentence is about speaking. If the problem is that you cannot follow what is being said to you, that is a different line — 我听不懂 says the words are not arriving, and answering with 我不会说中文 gets you English instead of slower Chinese.
Chinese has no fixed apology to bolt onto it. The sentence is blunt by design and works as the opening move; put 不好意思 in front only when you are cutting somebody off mid explanation.

replies.en: No problem, I'll speak more slowly.
Then let me write it out for you.

replies.py: Nǐ děng yíxià, wǒ zhǎo gè huì de.
replies.en: Wait a moment, I'll find someone who can.

when: When you need one small thing done right now — reading a sign aloud, holding a bag while you tie a shoe, or working out which platform a train leaves from.
Ask somebody who is standing still and whose job is being there, because a station counter or a hotel desk can act while a passer-by can only point.

variants.en: Could you give me a hand?
variants.note: The question version. 能 leaves the other person room to say no, which is what makes it usable with strangers.
帮我 plus a verb builds any small errand: 帮我看看 (have a look), 帮我拿一下 (hold this), 帮我读一下 (read this out).
请教 is the ask-in-order-to-learn verb. It is the polite way into a language question, where 帮我 is for an action.

mistakes: 一下 is the polite half, not 请. 请帮我 sounds formal and stiff — the register of a notice or a service desk — and dropping 一下 is what turns the request into a bare instruction.
一下 promises a small, finishable favour. Asking a stranger to watch your bags for an hour is not 一下, and the phrase will sound like you are understating what you actually want.
帮我一下 asks for an action; 我问一下 asks for an answer. At a station counter the second is often all you need, and it is the lighter way in — 我问一下，这个站台对吗？

replies.en: Sure, let me have a look.

when: Use it on a tour, in a hired car or with a group when nobody has told you the departure time yet and you need to plan your morning around it.
It is also the question for a bus or train station where the boards are not in English, and for the moment a driver says 等一下 — wait a bit — since that answer can mean ten minutes or two hours.

variants.note: 几点 asks for a clock time, while 什么时候 leaves it open.
走 is the everyday verb for leaving; 出发 is the one printed on timetables.

variants.en: How much longer do we wait?
variants.note: The follow-up to use when the first answer turns out to be vague.

mistakes: 走 means leaving, not departing on a schedule. 什么时候走 covers a person heading off, so keep 出发 for the official departure of a bus, train or tour.
If you are the one being asked, a bare number is not an answer. 八 is "eight", 八点 is "eight o'clock", and only the second one answers this question.
Chinese has no future tense, so the same sentence covers today and next week. Add 明天 or 后天 when the day matters.

replies.py: Děng rén qí le zài shuō.

when: Use it at the hotel front desk, ideally while laying your passport on the counter — hotels in China must register every guest, foreigners included, so the passport comes out either way.
It works with or without a booking: add 我有预订 (I have a reservation) if you booked ahead, or just say it as-is and the desk will ask what kind of room you want.

variants.note: 预订 is the booking you made ahead; pair it with your name — the name on the passport is how the desk will look it up.
办理入住 is the full formal collocation, the one printed on the desk sign — the polite, slightly ceremonial way to say it.
Many hotels take a refundable cash deposit (押金) at check-in and hand it back at check-out — asking first avoids the surprise.

mistakes: 入住 (rùzhù) is the check-in verb; 住宿 (zhùsù) means lodging in general and is what you see on signs and receipts. Check in with 入住, talk about lodging with 住宿.
Registration covers every guest, not just the one paying — all companions need their passports at the desk, even for a room booked for two.

The room key is 房卡 (fángkǎ, room card) in most hotels, not 钥匙 (yàoshi, key) — and when the card later fails to open the door, 房卡刷不开 (the room card won't swipe) is the phrase that brings you back to the desk.

replies.en: How many nights will you stay?

replies.zh: 这是您的房卡，早餐在二楼。
replies.py: Zhè shì nín de fángkǎ, zǎocān zài èrlóu.
replies.en: Here is your room card — breakfast is on the second floor.

when: Say it at the front desk when your stay is over and your bags are packed, and hand the key card across while you say it.
退 means to hand back, so 退房 is literally return the room — the same 退 you use in 退货 when returning goods to a shop.

variants.note: 现在 pins the moment — useful when the desk assumes you have one more night.
房卡 (room card) is the electronic key; older places may still hand you a metal 钥匙.

variants.py: Néng bāng wǒ jiào liàng chūzūchē ma?
variants.en: Can you call me a taxi?
variants.note: Front desks call taxis all morning — the natural next sentence after handing over the card.

mistakes: 退房 is only for the end of a stay — arriving is 入住. Walk up to the desk saying 退房 at check-in and it will assume you have lost a night somewhere.
A deposit paid at check-in comes back at this desk, not into your bank account — keep the deposit receipt, because the clerk may ask for it before handing back the cash.
Some hotels run a quick 查房 (room check) for the minibar before returning the deposit — it is routine housekeeping, not an accusation, and usually takes only a few minutes.

replies.en: Okay, let me take your key card.

replies.py: Xūyào bāng nín jiào chē ma?
replies.en: Do you need me to call a car?

when: Ask it at a hotel desk, café or restaurant the moment you need to get online, and staff will usually point at the password on a card or read it out.
Wi-Fi is said almost exactly as in English, so the only new word here is 有 — the all-purpose is-there question that starts thousands of Chinese sentences.

variants.note: 密码 covers every password you will type — Wi-Fi, phone unlock and payment PIN alike.
无线网 is the fully Chinese name for Wi-Fi — useful when the English letters alone stall the conversation.
不上 after a verb means the action will not complete — the same pattern as 买不到 (can't buy).

mistakes: 密码 (mìmǎ) is every kind of password or PIN — the card reader at checkout will ask for 密码 too, so hearing it at the register is not another Wi-Fi question.
Many cafés hand out the code printed on the receipt after you order, and hotel passwords usually live on the card in the room — looking there first can save the question entirely.
网 is not one fixed word: 无线网 is wireless internet, 上网 is to go online, and 网上 means online — the same character doing three different jobs.

replies.zh: 密码在桌上的小牌子上。
replies.py: Mìmǎ zài zhuō shàng de xiǎo páizi shàng.
replies.en: The password is on the little card on the table.
The password is your room number.

replies.zh: 这边信号不好，您坐那边吧。
replies.py: Zhèbiān xìnhào bù hǎo, nín zuò nàbiān ba.
replies.en: The signal is weak on this side — sit over there.

when: Say it at the front desk when the room is too hot or too cold and you have worked out that the machine is not responding at all, rather than that you cannot find the remote.
It is also the sentence to bring to a landlord or a homestay host, because 坏了 reports a fault without blaming anyone for it.

variants.note: Use it when the unit is running but blowing warm air — a different fault from a dead one.
打不开 covers anything that refuses to open or start, from a window to an app.

variants.py: Néng pài rén lái kànkan ma?
variants.en: Could you send someone to look at it?
variants.note: The follow-up that turns a report into an actual repair.

mistakes: 坏 is for things, never for people. 我坏了 is nonsense while 空调坏了 is normal, and the pattern takes any appliance: 灯坏了, 马桶坏了, 洗衣机坏了.
了 here is not past tense. 坏了 reports a new state — it has become broken — which is why the same sentence still describes a machine that is broken right now.
坏了 covers a machine that has failed. A device that has simply run out of power is 没电了 (méi diàn le), and saying 坏了 about a flat remote invites a repair visit you do not need.

replies.py: Hǎo de, wǒ mǎshàng jiào rén shàngqu.
replies.en: OK, I'll send someone up right away.

replies.py: Nín yào bu yào huàn ge fángjiān?
replies.en: Would you like to change rooms?

when: Use it in your hotel room when the towels are missing or you want a fresh set — call the front desk or catch housekeeping in the corridor, either way the phrase is the same.
Chinese hotels normally stock bath towels as standard, so if there are none the request is completely ordinary; it is housekeeping's job, not a favor.

variants.py: Qǐng zài gěi wǒ yì tiáo máojīn.
variants.en: Please bring me one more towel.
variants.note: 再 (again, more) plus the measure word 条 — towels are counted with 条, and this is the phrase for a second one.
浴巾 (yùjīn) is the big bath towel; plain 毛巾 can mean the small face towel. Naming the right one saves a trip.

variants.py: Qǐng sòng yì tiáo yùjīn lái.
variants.en: Please send up a bath towel.
variants.note: 送 is the natural verb on the phone — it means deliver to the room. 请给我毛巾 works face to face; 送 works across the building.

mistakes: Towels take the measure word 条 (tiáo), not 个 (gè). 一条毛巾 is right; 一个毛巾 marks you instantly.
毛巾 is the generic word and leans small — the bath sheet is 浴巾. Hotels provide bath towels but rarely washcloths, so a request for a tiny one may genuinely have no answer.
On the phone, the shape locals use is 请送一条到 808 房 (please send one to room 808) — 请给我毛巾 with no room number just leaves the desk asking which room you are in.

replies.en: We'll bring it up right away.

replies.py: Nín de fángjiān hào shì duōshao?

replies.en: The towels are on the rack in the bathroom.

when: Street markets, night markets, souvenir stalls and small independent shops: anywhere the price is spoken rather than printed.
Point at one specific item as you say it, because 这个 does the work of the noun you do not know.

variants.note: The market version, asking the rate rather than the total. You will hear it more than 多少钱 at fruit and vegetable stalls.
一斤 (yì jīn) is 500 grams, and fresh food in China is priced by it rather than by the item.

variants.en: Do you have a cheaper one?
variants.note: Moves the conversation from the price to the choice, which works in shops that stock several grades of the same thing.

mistakes: Say duōshao as one word. 少 keeps its third tone on its own but flattens inside 多少, so splitting the two syllables sounds wrong.
Ask about 这个 or 那个, never about nothing. In a crowded stall a bare 多少钱 makes the seller guess which of twenty items you mean.
In a supermarket the price is on the shelf tag and there is nothing to ask. This phrase earns its keep where prices are actually spoken.

when: Say it in markets, night stalls and tourist streets, and say it with a smile — in those places the first price is an opening, so asking for less is expected rather than rude.
Expect to settle somewhere in the middle, and expect the answer to be a number rather than a word: the seller usually replies with a price, not with a yes.

variants.py: Néng bù néng zài shǎo yìdiǎn?
variants.en: Could you go a little lower?
variants.note: 少 (less) is the word that fits price talk — 少一点 is "a bit less". The 能不能 frame asks permission, which softens it further.
The move that works when a flat discount does not: buy more, pay less each. It also shifts the subject from your budget to the seller's volume.

variants.en: Come down a bit more and I'll take it.
variants.note: Names the trade instead of repeating the ask. 就 here means "then" — a lower price produces a purchase, and that is the sentence a seller listens for.

mistakes: 便宜一点 is not the same as 打折: 打折 asks about a promotion the seller already has, 便宜一点 asks the seller to move the price for you.
一点 is doing real work — the request is deliberately small. 可以便宜吗 with no 一点 sounds like a challenge to the prices themselves, and it tends to be met with a flat no.
The first answer is very often 不行 or 不能便宜. That is a position rather than a refusal, and saying the same words again more loudly does not move it — changing the offer does.

replies.py: Zhège jià yǐjīng hěn piányi le.

when: Ask it in a clothing shop when you want to use the fitting room — in many smaller shops the staff will unlock one for you rather than leaving them open.
It is also the phrase for trying anything on or out in front of the seller, from shoes to sunglasses to a phone case, where English would reach for several different verbs.

variants.note: 试穿 is specifically for clothes, so it is the safest choice in a clothing shop.

variants.en: May I give it a try?
variants.note: 试一下 carries the same meaning without the doubling; the repeated 试试 sounds softer and more casual.
The natural follow-up as soon as the answer is yes.

mistakes: 试 is not the exam word. 试 means trying something on or out, while 考试 is sitting a test, so 我可以考试吗 in a shop gets a blank look.
The fitting room is 试衣间 as one unit. 试衣 alone does not name a room, and 更衣室 is a changing room for sport, so staff will point you somewhere else.
Do not use this to mean you are still deciding. 试 is a physical try-on; to say you will think it over, use 考虑 (kǎolǜ).

replies.en: Sure, the fitting room is over there.
You can only try two pieces.
This one can't be tried on.

when: You say it to a shop assistant who comes over as you walk in: it tells them you are not ready to buy and that you will ask if you need anything.
Because it is a soft no, it works on touts and street sellers too — said with a smile it ends the pitch without making the person feel brushed off.

variants.note: Sharper and shorter. 就 narrows it to 'only', so this version says the looking is all you intend to do.
Drops the 我 and is what you hear from local shoppers. Fine on its own, though with no pronoun it can sound abrupt to an older assistant.

variants.en: I'll call you if I need anything.
variants.note: The line that actually releases you. Adding it after 我随便看看 gives the assistant something to do other than follow you around.

mistakes: 随便 does not mean 'whatever' here. 随便 on its own in answer to a question (what do you want to eat?) sounds careless; inside 我随便看看 it means 'casually', which is what makes the phrase friendly.
It is an answer to the assistant, not a refusal of the shop. Say it and they will usually stay nearby rather than leave you alone.
看看 is a doubled verb, so it means 'have a look around' rather than 'look'. The same doubling softens 试试 (try it), 走走 (walk around) and 想想 (think it over).

replies.en: Call me if you need anything.
You can try this one on.

when: Use it at the counter before you open your wallet, when you cannot see a card machine and want to know whether one exists at all.
In China the answer is often neither card nor cash but a QR code — Alipay and WeChat Pay dominate daily payments, and small shops may have no card reader at all.

variants.note: Asking where rather than whether already assumes the answer is yes — useful in supermarkets, where a machine certainly exists but is hidden around a pillar.
The everyday question in China. It covers Alipay, WeChat Pay and phone wallets in one phrase, without naming any app.
When the counter only shows a QR code, this asks whether pointing your camera at it really is the whole payment.

mistakes: 刷卡 literally means brush a card — the verb for using a card is 刷 (shuā), so 刷卡机 is the card machine and 刷卡 is the act. 用卡 is understandable but nobody says it at a counter.

Card usually means UnionPay (银联 yínlián) in China. Many readers take nothing else, so a foreign Visa or Mastercard can fail even when the answer to 可以刷卡吗 is yes — which is exactly why Alipay and WeChat Pay are the safer default.
刷卡 covers debit cards too, not just credit. If you specifically mean the credit kind, that word is 信用卡 (xìnyòngkǎ).

when: Say it while holding up the garment whose size does not fit, so the staff can see which piece you mean and fetch the next size from the stockroom.
Clothing sizes are 小号 (small), 中号 (medium) and 大号 (large), and most shops keep other sizes in the back rather than on the rack.

variants.note: The three rack grades are fixed: 小号 S, 中号 M, 大号 L — learn one and you have learned all three.

variants.py: Yǒu dà yí hào de ma?
variants.en: Do you have one size up?
variants.note: 号 counts size steps: 大一号 is one size bigger, 小一号 is one size smaller.

variants.en: Does it come in other sizes?
variants.note: 尺码 is the general word for garment sizes, useful when you want the whole range rather than one grade.

mistakes: 小号 means size S on a clothing rack, but the same word is also a small cup at a drink stand or a trumpet in an orchestra — holding up the garment removes every doubt about which you mean.
Size racks and size labels are always the grade names 小号 / 中号 / 大号, not adjectives — asking 这个有小的吗 points at small things in sight, not at the size grade.
Chinese sizes usually run smaller than US or EU sizes, so the 中号 that fits you at home may pinch here — check the numbered label (the 165/88A style) or try the piece on before paying.

replies.en: Let me grab one from the back.

replies.py: Jiù shèng zhè yí jiàn le.
replies.en: This is the only one left.

when: Say it at the checkout after paying, when the cashier is about to hand over your things loose and you need something to carry them in.
Supermarkets often give bags free, while many smaller shops charge a few cents for one — the cashier will ask 要袋子吗 at the register, and this sentence answers that question before it comes.

variants.note: 塑料袋 names the plastic bag specifically — the kind you get at a checkout.
Refusing saves the bag fee where shops charge, and it is the answer to 要袋子吗 when you already have one.
免费 (free of charge) is worth knowing everywhere, not just at a checkout.

mistakes: The bag you carry is 袋子, but 袋 alone is a measure word: 一袋米 is a bag of rice. The 子 ending is what turns the measure word into the object itself.
要袋子吗 at the register is a routine checkout question, not an upsell — answer 要 or 不用 and nothing more is needed.
For takeaway food the word is 打包, not 袋子 — leftovers leave a restaurant in a 打包盒, shopping bags come from shop checkouts, and each scene keeps its own word.

replies.py: Yào dà de háishi xiǎo de?
Dàizi yào jiā yí kuài qián.
replies.en: The bag costs one yuan extra.

when: Use it at the shop counter when you are handing back something you bought and want your money back, receipt in hand.
Chinese shops rarely take returns without the receipt (发票 fāpiào), so keep it until you are sure you are keeping the item — no receipt usually means no return.

variants.note: 退掉 adds 掉, the completive ending — it sounds slightly more decided, like the matter is closed once you say it.

variants.py: Zhège yǒu wèntí, wǒ yào tuì.
variants.en: There is a problem with this — I'm returning it.
variants.note: Stating the reason in the same breath makes the request harder to wave away; 有问题 (there is a problem) is all the explanation you need.

variants.en: Can I exchange it for another one?
variants.note: 换 is exchange. Exchanges are easier than refunds in China, so if you only want a working item, ask with 换 before saying 退.

mistakes: The word on the shop sign is 退货 (tuìhuò, return goods). 退这个 works fine in conversation, but if staff look uncertain, 退货 is the category word that settles what you want.
退 is for giving something back to a shop; 还 (huán) is for returning something you borrowed from a person. 还给朋友 means give it back to my friend — using 退 there turns a favor into a business dispute.
If you specifically want money back rather than a replacement, that word is 退款 (tuìkuǎn, refund). 我要退款 tells the staff you are not interested in exchanging.

replies.py: Zhǐ néng huàn, bù néng tuì.

when: Ask it in markets, small shops and tourist streets, where the seller sets the price rather than a head office. In a mall or a chain store the staff have no authority to change a posted price, so the answer there is always the same.
The word itself is the tell: 打折 is a reduction the seller is running, so a yes means a posted price comes down — it does not mean bargaining has started.

variants.note: The follow-up to a yes. In Chinese pricing 折 counts what is left of the original, so 九折 pays 90% and 八折 pays 80% — a bigger number is a smaller discount.
Covers vouchers and member prices rather than a flat reduction. 优惠 is the word you see on posters, in apps and at the till in chain stores.

variants.en: Is there anything on at the moment?
variants.note: 活动 (an event or campaign) is what shops call a seasonal sale. It is the everyday way to ask, and it applies to restaurants and cinemas as well as shops.

mistakes: 打折 is not a synonym for haggling. It asks whether the seller already has a promotion; when you want the price itself moved, that is 便宜一点 (make it cheaper).
Chinese discounts count what you pay, not what you save. 九折 is pay-90%, 八折 is pay-80% — the opposite of how "20% off" reads.
Three words get confused: 打折 is a seller's reduction, 优惠 is a promotion or perk, and 便宜 simply means cheap. 大优惠 on a shop window is a deal that already exists, not one you can ask for.

when: The standard greeting at any hour of the day, with anyone you do not know well.
It is also how people answer the phone in Chinese.

variants.note: Same sentence with the formal 您 instead of 你. Use it with much older people, doctors, and anyone serving you in a formal setting.
Casual. Common among younger people and in messaging.

mistakes: 你好 is for first meetings and formal moments. Greeting a friend with it every morning sounds distant — friends often greet each other with a comment or nothing at all.
Do not treat it as 'how are you'. 你好吗 is a literal question people rarely ask; everyday greetings are usually observations about what you can see.

when: Thank someone for anything small: handing you change, pouring tea, letting you pass, holding a door.
It works everywhere in China — shops, taxis, hotels, friends. It is never too formal and never too casual.

variants.note: Adding 你 makes it directed at one specific person — slightly warmer and more personal.
For real help: someone carried your bag, waited for you, or went out of their way.

mistakes: Say it once, at the end. English speakers tend to sprinkle thanks through a sentence; in Chinese one 谢谢 at the close is plenty.
谢谢 never means 'please'. To ask for something politely use 请 (qǐng), or just state what you want with a calm tone.

when: To apologise for something real: bumping into someone, arriving late, breaking something.
Also used to politely interrupt or to get past someone in a crowd.

variants.note: The light apology, and far more common in daily life than 对不起. Use it for asking someone to move, interrupting, being a few minutes late.
A step more formal. Frequent in writing and in semi-formal speech.

mistakes: Do not reach for 对不起 every time English would use 'sorry'. For small daily friction — squeezing past someone, asking a stranger to repeat themselves — 不好意思 sounds natural where 对不起 feels heavy, as if you caused real trouble.
Do not confuse it with the reply. When someone apologises to you, the answer is 没关系 (méi guānxi, "it's fine"), not another apology.

when: The standard answer to 谢谢. Say it whenever someone thanks you for something you did.
It also means 'don't stand on ceremony' when you are urging someone to help themselves.

variants.note: Soft and very common — the everyday default.
Casual. Good among friends and younger people.

mistakes: The most useful thing to know: many people in China answer 谢谢 with no words at all, or with a small gesture or nod. Silence here is not rudeness.
Do not answer thanks with 哪里哪里 (nǎlǐ nǎlǐ). That is a modest reply to a compliment — using it after 谢谢 would be answering the wrong kind of remark.

when: When you leave a shop, a taxi, a restaurant or someone's home — the all-purpose goodbye that works anywhere.
Also on the phone before hanging up, and when you part from someone you will not see again soon.

variants.note: Borrowed from 'bye-bye' and very common among friends and younger people. Fine in casual settings, a little light for a formal farewell.
Literally 'see you when I turn my head'. For people you genuinely expect to meet again.
The normal way to announce you are leaving a group — a dinner table, an office, a party. It comes before 再见, not instead of it.

mistakes: 再见 works when both sides are leaving. To step away for a moment — leaving your table to ask a question — say 我去问一下 (wǒ qù wèn yíxià, "I'll go and ask") and come back.
Do not overuse it. Chinese speakers often leave a shop with a nod, or with 谢谢, and nothing else. 再见 every single time sounds earnest rather than wrong.

when: With someone you already know — a friend, a colleague, a host you have met before. It is a real question about how they have been.
Not the right opener with a stranger. With a shopkeeper, a driver or hotel staff the greeting is 你好 on its own; 你好吗 there sounds like a line from a textbook.

variants.note: What people actually say to a friend or colleague they have not seen for a while.
Use it when it really has been a long time. It replaces the question rather than leading into it.
An old greeting, not an invitation to dinner. Common among neighbours and older people — 吃了 or 还没 is a complete answer.

mistakes: 你好吗 is textbook Chinese. It appears in teaching material and in what Chinese speakers say to learners; between two native speakers you will hear 最近怎么样, or a remark about something they can see.
Do not answer with 我很好，谢谢，你呢. That is the textbook dialogue. 挺好的 or 还行 is what a real answer sounds like.
It is also not a greeting for the phone. Chinese speakers answer the phone with 喂 (wéi).

when: You ask it of someone your own age — a fellow traveller, a new colleague, a host's friend — where the direct form is completely normal.
To somebody older, or to anyone whose name you need for a form, the polite version is 您贵姓 (nín guìxìng) — the direct question can sound like you are checking up on them.

variants.note: 请问 in front is all it takes to move the same sentence from casual to polite. This is the safe version at a hotel or an office.
The formal question, used with older people and in business. 贵 is a courtesy word: literally 'your honourable surname'.
The easiest one to use, because it asks only what to call the person rather than for a full name. Very common in workplaces.

mistakes: 名字 is the full name; surname and given name are separate words. 姓 is the family name and it comes first — in 王小明, 王 is the 姓 and 小明 the given name — and 您贵姓 asks only for the 姓.
The question already contains 什么, so it takes no 吗. Adding one (你叫什么名字吗) is the mistake foreigners make most often with this sentence.
Do not build it as 你的名字是什么. It is a word-for-word translation of 'what is your name'; it is understood, but the natural sentence uses 叫.

when: When someone speaks too fast, uses words you do not know, or explains something technical.
It works best paired with a gesture — pointing, or turning your phone around. People usually slow down, switch to simpler words, or start writing characters.

variants.note: More precise when the problem is speed, accent or audio quality rather than the words themselves.

variants.py: Nǐ shuō màn yìdiǎn, hǎo ma?
variants.en: Could you say it a bit slower?
variants.note: The follow-up that actually fixes the problem.

mistakes: 不懂 is about understanding, not ability. 'I can't speak Chinese' is 我不会说中文 (wǒ bú huì shuō Zhōngwén). Saying 我不懂中文 says you understand nothing at all, which understates you.
If you are interrupting someone to say it, lead with 不好意思.

when: Say it when someone has spoken and you caught the sound but not the meaning. This sentence asks them to repeat exactly the same thing rather than to explain it differently.
It is the polite default with anyone you have just met, and it works on the phone as well as face to face, where a bare 什么？ would sound abrupt.

variants.en: Please say it one more time.
variants.note: 次 counts any occurrence while 遍 counts a run from start to finish, which is why 遍 fits speech better.

variants.py: Méi tīng qīng, zài shuō yí biàn.
variants.en: I didn't catch that, say it again.
variants.note: Leading with 没听清 explains why you are asking, which softens the request.

variants.zh: 不好意思，再说一遍好吗？
variants.py: Bù hǎoyìsi, zài shuō yí biàn hǎo ma?
variants.en: Sorry, could you say that again?
variants.note: 不好意思 in front and 好吗 at the end makes this the most polite version of the request.

mistakes: 遍 cannot count anything that happens in time. 三遍 is three readings of the same thing from start to finish, while three separate trips to a shop are 三次.
再 and 又 both look like "again" but they are not interchangeable. 再说一遍 asks for the next repetition, while 又说一遍 describes someone repeating themselves.
Do not shorten it to 什么？ outside your own circle. Among friends it is fine, but with anyone else it reads as surprise or irritation rather than a request.

replies.py: Hǎo de, wǒ zài shuō yí biàn.

replies.en: Let me put it another way.

when: To get a stranger's attention before a question: hotel staff, a passer-by, someone behind a counter.
It also covers squeezing past somebody, interrupting a conversation and making a light apology for something small, which is why you hear it dozens of times a day in China.

variants.en: Excuse me, may I ask something?
variants.note: The full opener: attention first, question marker second. The safest way to start with someone you do not know.
Slightly more formal. Good when you need real help from someone at a desk or a service counter.
The serious apology. 不好意思 is for brushing past somebody; 对不起 is for having actually done something wrong.

mistakes: It is not only an apology. Most of the time it opens a conversation, so say it before the question rather than after you have been refused.
Do not spend it on something serious. Knock over a display or damage an item and 对不起 is the phrase; 不好意思 sounds far too light.

It doubles as a polite refusal: 不好意思，我不需要 is how you wave off a tout at a tourist site without being rude. Staff will also say it to you when they have no tables left, and it is a softener rather than bad news.

when: Ask it when the menu is long, the characters are unfamiliar and you would rather trust the server than guess.
推荐 means to recommend, and in a busy restaurant the answer is usually one or two dishes the kitchen is known for, not a tour of the whole menu.

variants.note: 招牌 is the shop's signboard — 招牌菜 is literally the dish they hang their name on.
特色 highlights what is distinctive about this kitchen, often what is local to the region.

variants.py: Nǎge diǎn de rén zuì duō?
variants.note: The best-seller question — crowd wisdom instead of one person's taste, and the easiest for a busy server to answer.

mistakes: 推荐 is not only about food — hotels, apps and walking routes all take it, so the pattern 有什么推荐 works again the next day at the hotel desk.
“What's good here” maps to two different questions — 哪个最好卖 (which sells best) and 什么最好吃 (which tastes best) — and the honest answers can differ.
If the recommendation is expensive, the server will usually say so outright; following up with 有便宜一点的吗 is a normal question in China, not an insult to the kitchen.

replies.py: Zhège diǎn de rén zuì duō.
replies.en: This one gets ordered the most.

when: Use it while ordering, before any dish is chosen, so the waiter can point you at the 素菜 (vegetarian) part of the menu instead of watching you reject dishes one by one.
One short syllable of 素 is easy to miss in a noisy room, so add 不要肉 (no meat) if the first answer looks uncertain — the two together are what staff actually act on.

variants.note: The full, explicit version. 素食 (vegetarian food) is also the word printed on menus and product labels, so you will see it even if you never say it.
素菜 is the menu category — it skips the statement about yourself and goes straight to what you want on the table.
放 is the cooking verb to add. Say this when a dish you otherwise want sounds like it might have meat stirred in.

mistakes: On Chinese menus, 肉 by itself usually means pork. Chicken is 鸡肉 and fish is just 鱼, and staff may not count either as 肉 — if you avoid them too, name them: 不吃鸡肉和鱼.
素菜 usually means no meat in the dish, but it may still be cooked with 蚝油 (háoyóu, oyster sauce) or meat stock. If that matters to you, ask 有蚝油吗？ (does it have oyster sauce?)
Say it at ordering time, not when the dish lands. Kitchens rarely rebuild a plate mid-meal, and the vegetarian dishes often need to be ordered as their own dish in the first place.

replies.en: Sure — the vegetarian dishes are here.

when: As the answer to a question built on 是: 这是你的吗？ (Is this yours?), 你是老师吗？ (Are you a teacher?). Here 是 means 'it is' or 'I am'.
Also to confirm something someone has just said about themselves or about the situation.

variants.note: The most common way to say 'yes' to a statement in Chinese. When you are unsure which word to use, 对 is the safe one.
Softer and less clipped than a bare 是.

mistakes: Chinese has no single word for 'yes'. You answer by repeating the verb from the question: 有吗 → 有, 去吗 → 去, 可以吗 → 可以, 喜欢吗 → 喜欢. A bare 是 to a question that did not use 是 sounds wrong.
是 links two nouns: 他是老师 (he is a teacher). It is not used with adjectives — those take 很 instead. 她很漂亮 is right, 她是漂亮 is not. This is one of the most persistent habits carried over from English.

when: As the negative answer to a 是 question: 这是你的吗？ 不是。
Also to correct something wrong: 不是，我是英国人 (No — I'm British).

variants.note: Softer than a bare 不是, which can land bluntly in a conversation.

variants.en: I don't have it. / It didn't happen.
variants.note: The right 'no' for 有 questions and for things that did not happen. Not interchangeable with 不是.
For correcting information, not for answering a 是 question.

mistakes: 不是 negates 是 only. To refuse something offered — in a shop, a taxi, at a table — the polite form is 不用了，谢谢, not 不是.
Watch the tone. 不 is normally bù, but it turns into bú before a 4th tone: it is bú shì, not bù shì. The same happens in 不对 (bú duì) and 不用 (bú yòng).
不是 and 没 are not interchangeable. 没 (or 没有) is for things that did not happen or that you do not have; 不是 is for saying what something is not.

when: You put it in front of any question you ask a stranger — shop staff, a station attendant, somebody on the street — and a bare question turns into a polite opener.
It also works as the attention-getter on its own: say 请问 and pause, and the person will look up before you have said what you want.

variants.note: 一下 softens it further and buys you a moment to finish the sentence. Very common when you are about to ask for directions.

variants.en: Sorry to trouble you, may I ask?
variants.note: 麻烦 (to put somebody to trouble) makes the request more considerate. Good at a service counter where the person is already busy.
The no-frills version, used between younger people and in shops where 请问 would sound stiff. 一下 does the softening instead.

mistakes: It goes in front of a full question, not instead of one. 请问 alone means 'may I ask', so the other person stops and waits — have the question ready before you start.
It is polite, not warm. 请问 keeps an exchange businesslike, which is exactly right with staff and wrong with a friend: used on somebody you know it sounds like a call centre.
Tone, not volume, carries it. 请 is a full third tone and 问 is falling, so flattening the two into 'qing-wen' is the tell that you have read the phrase rather than heard it.

replies.py: Bù hǎoyìsi, wǒ yě bù zhīdào.

when: Before about 10 a.m. — to hotel staff, a shopkeeper, a taxi driver, your host.
On arriving somewhere in the morning: a shop, a waiting room, a friend's home. It is a greeting, never a goodbye.

variants.note: The one-word version. Everyone understands it, and friends will often answer with it.
Correct and understood, but 你好 is far more common in the afternoon — this one sounds deliberate.
For arriving somewhere in the evening. Not a farewell.
Only when parting for the night or going to bed. Never a greeting.

mistakes: 早上好 has a window. Mid-morning onwards it sounds off — switch to 你好, which works at any hour.
Do not use 晚上好 to say goodbye. 晚安 is the farewell; 晚上好 is only for arriving.
Greeting a friend with 早上好 every single morning sounds formal. Friends often just acknowledge each other — 来了 (you're here) — and start talking.

when: You say it when you are going to bed, or when you are the one leaving late: it is a farewell, so it closes a conversation rather than opening one.
Chinese uses it less than English uses 'good night', so it can sound a little formal; among friends a plain 我先睡了 (I'm going to sleep first) is the everyday version.

variants.note: The way a chat actually ends at night. 先 makes it 'before you', which is what turns it into a soft exit rather than an announcement.
What people say instead of good night when the other person is still working. It is a wish for their health, so it does not end the conversation.
好梦 is the standard addition, used with family and close friends. The longer written form is 祝你做个好梦.

mistakes: 晚安 is not the evening greeting. Arriving at a hotel or meeting somebody after dark, the word is 晚上好 (wǎnshang hǎo) — 晚安 there would tell them you are going to bed.
Chinese greets by time of day: 早上好, 下午好, 晚上好. 晚安 is the only one of the four used at the end of the day rather than the start, which is why mixing it up is the classic slip.
In writing it is everywhere — messages, posts, customer-service sign-offs. In speech it is mostly between family and partners, so it lands warmer than 晚上好 does.

replies.en: OK, you get some sleep too.

when: When you accept an offer or agree to a plan: a driver checks the address, a waiter suggests a dish, a friend tells you where to meet.
Also a soft 'all right, go ahead' when someone is explaining something to you.

variants.note: Shorter and more decisive. Common in quick exchanges, but can sound clipped with someone you have just met.
Very common in northern China. 行 is about whether something is workable, so it answers 'is this OK?' rather than 'do you want it?'
The safest 'yes' to a proposal — it carries permission rather than enthusiasm.
For when someone is asking you to do something.

mistakes: 好的 and 好吧 are not the same. 好吧 means 'all right then' and carries reluctance — saying it when you mean 好的 sounds as though you were talked into something.
好的 agrees with a proposal. It is not a general 'yes': for a 是 question you need 是 or 对.
It is easy to overuse. After a while 好 on its own sounds more natural, and between friends a nod is enough.

when: When you genuinely have nothing to give — somebody asking you for directions, for a shop's opening hours, or about a place you are also visiting for the first time.
It is a plain statement, not a request for slower speech: 我不懂 asks for a rephrase, while 我不知道 says the answer is not in your hands.

variants.note: 也 does a lot of work here. It tells the other person you are not withholding anything — you are in the same position they are.
清楚 is 'clear', so 不清楚 reports uncertainty rather than a flat blank. Softer than 不知道 without being vague.

variants.en: Let me ask someone for you.
variants.note: The closing move when you want to help anyway. Doubling the verb (问问) is what makes the errand sound casual rather than a favour you are owed.

mistakes: 不知道 answers a question you understood. If the words themselves did not land, it sounds like a refusal to answer and people will simply repeat the question louder — 我不懂 is the one that asks for a rephrase.
不太 needs a gradable word after it. 我不太清楚 is correct and softer, while 我不太知道 is a slip; it is a common one, because 不知道 is so frequent that it feels safe to soften.

There is no bare yes to fall back on when somebody checks something with you. If you mean 'I have heard of it' rather than 'I know', 我听说过 is the verb — and 我知道 as a two-word answer can sound like 'obviously I know'.

replies.en: No problem, I'll ask someone else.
You can ask at the front desk.

when: When you want to set expectations before the conversation goes wrong — a hotel desk, a clinic, a bank counter, or anyone who starts at full speed.
Saying it up front works better than asking for a repeat later, because it changes how the other person picks their words from the first sentence.

variants.note: 一般 is the standard Chinese way of saying 'nothing special'. It is more understated, and more native-sounding, than 不好.
听得懂 is 'hear and understand'. Splitting 听 (hear) from 懂 (understand) is what lets you tell people which half is failing.

variants.py: Qǐng shuō màn yìdiǎn kěyǐ ma?
variants.en: Could you speak a little more slowly?
variants.note: The slow-down request framed as a question, which gives the other person room to decline. Easier to say to a stranger than a bare 请说慢一点.

mistakes: The 得 is doing real work. It links 说 to how well the speaking is done, so 说得不好 reports on this conversation rather than on your ceiling. Drop it and 我说不好 starts to sound like a verdict on yourself.
The answer you will get is 你中文说得很好, and it is politeness rather than a measurement. Agreeing looks odd and arguing looks worse; 谢谢，还在学 is what the line expects.
No apology is needed. Chinese has no fixed version of 'sorry, my Chinese is bad' as an opener, and adding 对不起 turns a neutral request into a confession about a language you are still learning.

replies.py: Nǐ Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo!

when: When you need to know whether the person across the counter can switch to English — a station ticket window, a hotel desk, a hospital reception.
会 asks about a learned skill, so this is a question about their English rather than a request for it; swapping in 能 turns it into 'could you say it in English right now'.

variants.note: 英语 and 英文 both mean English. 英文 is the more common word in speech; 英语 is the one on school timetables.

variants.en: Can we do this in English?
variants.note: Frames it as the situation rather than the person's ability, which is an easier yes to give.

variants.py: Yǒu huì shuō Yīngyǔ de rén ma?
variants.en: Is there anyone who speaks English?
variants.note: The escalator question. At a counter this gets you handed to a colleague instead of a shrug.

mistakes: A no from one person says nothing about the next one. English is a school subject in China and how much of it stayed varies a lot from person to person, so asking again down the queue is normal rather than rude.
Do not drop the 会. 你说英语吗 asks whether they are speaking English at this moment, which lands like a complaint about the language they just used; 你会说英语吗 asks about the skill.
It is a question, not an order. The tone people hear is 'is English possible here?', so a shrug at the answer is normal — the useful follow-up is 那请说慢一点 rather than the same sentence louder.

when: You say it to a partner, a parent, or your own child — 爱 covers family love as much as romantic love, so it is not reserved for one relationship.
Chinese uses it far less often than English uses 'I love you', so it carries weight: saying it out of the blue, rather than on an occasion, is itself the message.

variants.py: Wǒ zhēn de hěn ài nǐ.
variants.note: 真的很 is how Chinese adds 'really'. English puts the word in the same place, so this is the one line that maps almost word for word.
很 before 爱 adds intensity rather than being the flat 'very' of 很好. Order matters: 很 comes before the verb, so 我爱你很 is not a sentence.
The everyday word for liking, and what you say to a friend or early on. 喜欢 does not carry the weight of 爱, which is exactly why it is the safer choice.

mistakes: Saying it to a friend can land oddly. 爱 is the word for partners, parents and children; with a friend the natural phrase is 我很喜欢你 (I really like you), and 我爱你 between friends may be taken as a confession.
爱 takes things as well as people. 我爱吃辣 (I love spicy food) and 我爱这个地方 are ordinary, so hearing 爱 does not by itself signal romance — what signals it is the object being 你.
Chinese does not change the verb for the subject or the object, so 我爱你 is the same sentence whoever says it. 'I love you too' is therefore 我也爱你, with 也 before 爱.

when: At a table when the glasses come together: the same two words work as the invitation to drink and as the answer to one.
Not only formal dinners. It is the ordinary toast among friends, colleagues and family, and you will hear it several times in an evening.

variants.note: The short form of the same word. Very common at lively tables and it means exactly the same thing.

variants.en: I will finish mine, you drink as you like.
variants.note: The polite way to toast somebody who may not want to match you glass for glass.
敬 is the verb for toasting a person, used to a host, an elder or a guest of honour.

mistakes: 干杯 means empty the glass, not clink and sip. If you are not drinking alcohol, 我以茶代酒 (I will drink tea instead) is understood and accepted, and your glass stops being refilled.
There is an order to it. The host toasts first, and when a younger person toasts somebody older the glass is held slightly lower. Getting that right matters more than the word.
Toasting here is social rather than competitive. 随意 (as you like) is the standard escape hatch, and saying it once protects you for the rest of the evening.

when: To anyone on their birthday — a friend, a colleague, someone at the next table.
Very often written rather than spoken: on a card, on a red envelope, or in a chat message.

variants.note: The fuller form. 祝 is the verb 'to wish', so this reads as a formal wish rather than a shout.
Common with older people, where a wish for health carries more weight than the birthday itself.
The 啊 at the end makes it sound spoken and warm rather than read off a card.

mistakes: 生日快乐 is only for birthdays. The formula is occasion + 快乐: 新年快乐 (Happy New Year), 节日快乐 (happy holiday), 周末快乐 (have a good weekend). 快乐 always comes second.
It is said on the day, not in advance — there is no Chinese equivalent of 'many happy returns'.
The short version is the common one. Adding 祝你 makes it warmer in writing, not more correct in speech.

when: You say it as the answer to 对不起, and when somebody apologises for a small accident — bumping into you, stepping on your foot, knocking your bag.
It also closes a problem rather than accepting an apology: it says the whole thing has stopped mattering, so use it to end a complaint rather than to open one.

variants.note: The short everyday version, used constantly in speech. Fine after a bump in a crowd; too light for an apology that was meant seriously.
The warmer twin of 没关系. 要紧 means 'to matter', so 不要紧 is 'it doesn't matter' — you will hear staff use it to wave off an apology.
For something the other person feels genuinely bad about. 放在心上 is literally 'put it in your heart', so this is the phrase that actually forgives.

mistakes: It answers 对不起, not 谢谢. Reply to thanks with 不客气 — 没关系 after 谢谢 sounds as though you are forgiving the person rather than accepting their gratitude.
It dismisses the incident, not the person's feeling. If you want to say 'no harm done, but please be careful', 没关系 will not carry it, because it closes the topic.
Tone decides whether it lands. A flat 没关系 after a real apology reads as cold; the same words with 真 in front (真没关系) are what make the other person believe you.

replies.en: I'll be on my way then.

when: Say it when you need a few seconds — to find the word you want, to open a payment app, or to check the change. 请 in front keeps it a request and 一下 keeps it short.
It is the phrase for someone who is mid-task: a cashier ringing up your basket, a clerk already serving another customer, a driver stopped at a light.

variants.note: Drop the 请 and this is what friends and colleagues say to each other all day. To a stranger it can land as abrupt, so keep the 请 there.
The service-counter version. 稍 is the 稍 of 稍微 (slightly); you will hear it in shops, banks and on customer-service lines.
Buying time for a decision rather than for a task. The doubled 想想 makes it "think a little", which is softer than a flat 想.

mistakes: 等一下 is not rude on its own — tone carries it. Said flatly to a stranger it reads as an order; with 请 in front it is a request.
等一下 points at the task, not at you. To mean "wait for me" while you are the one walking ahead, Chinese says 等我一下 — 等我 (wait for me) plus 一下.
一 changes tone here: it is yī standing alone but yí before a fourth tone like xià. The same shift gives 一个 (yí ge) and 一次 (yí cì).

when: Say it to turn down something that is being offered — a tout at a station exit, a driver quoting a fare, an assistant holding up a second item.
The 谢谢 on the end matters more than it looks: it marks the refusal as a decision about the offer rather than a judgement about the person, and it gives them a clean place to stop.

variants.note: Flatter and more final than 不用了. In a crowd it is the one that ends the exchange fastest.
Turns the refusal into a fact about you rather than a verdict on the offer — useful when the same person asks a second and third time.
A soft brush-off for the second or third ask. 吧 makes it a suggestion rather than a closed door, which suits a street you might walk down again.

mistakes: 不用 is not a word-for-word "no thanks": 用 is "to need", so 不用 is "not needed". The literal sense is firmer than the English sounds, and the 谢谢 is what keeps it polite.
Chinese has no single word for "no". A flat 不 on its own sounds like a challenge; refusals come as 不用了, 不要了 or 不行, one situation at a time.
The 了 in 不用了 is doing work: it marks a decision being made now. 不用 without it can read as a general statement — "not needed" — rather than a reply to the offer in front of you.

replies.en: Come find me if you need anything.

when: Use it the moment you are introduced to someone — right after the handshake or the nod — as the standard way to open a new acquaintance in Chinese.
It also fits hosts, guides, hotel managers and a friend's parents, though people of your own age usually just say 你好 again and get straight to talking.

variants.note: The same words with the feeling first — this is the order you will hear most often.
Short and slightly formal; it belongs to exchanged business cards rather than parties.
见到 is about the meeting itself, so it fits the moment you go from messages to face to face.

mistakes: Not for service staff. You are not introduced to a waiter or a cashier, so 认识你很高兴 lands as oddly weighty there — a plain 你好 is what people actually say.
认识 is for people, 知道 is for facts. 我知道你 means "I know of you", which is a very different thing to say to someone you have just met.
幸会 does not mix with 很高兴. Pick one register and stay in it: 幸会幸会 for a card exchange, 很高兴认识你 for everybody else.

when: Say it early in a conversation you are struggling through. It reframes the whole exchange: once the person knows you are a visitor, they stop testing whether you understood and start explaining instead.
It is also the sentence that opens the door for help — knowing you do not know the local routine makes a follow-up question expected rather than an imposition.

variants.note: Works in the same places as 我是游客 but carries no holiday context — useful at a bank, a clinic or anywhere a clerk is deciding how much to explain.
刚 marks "only just". Adding it explains why you have no local number, no payment app set up and no idea of the routine yet.

variants.en: This is my first time here.
variants.note: The one that reliably gets patience and invites recommendations. 第一次 is the frame for any first time — 第一次来中国, 第一次吃火锅.

mistakes: 游客 means a sightseeing visitor. A business traveller is 出差 (chūchāi) and a student is 留学生, so 我是游客 is the wrong label on a work trip.
Saying it is a strategy, not a confession. Staff change register when they hear it: instructions get repeated, and answers come with the extra step that a local would have been expected to know.
It is a label, not an apology, so no 不好意思 is needed. English adds "sorry, I'm just a tourist"; in Chinese the sorry makes it sound like you are apologising for being there.

when: You say it reacting to good news: a table found, a plan confirmed, a problem somebody else just solved. It is genuine enthusiasm, not politeness.
It is also how you praise something you were given or shown — a dish, a photo, somebody's Chinese — where a plain 很好 would sound flat.

variants.note: The plain version of the same frame, and the one you will hear most. 好 is safe anywhere; 棒 is louder and younger.
A little more measured than 太棒了. 不错 is 'not bad', and with 真 in front it turns into real praise.
For a person's skill or effort rather than a piece of news. 厉害 is the standard compliment for somebody who just did something difficult.

mistakes: 太…了 needs the 了. 太棒 on its own is not a sentence; the unit is 太 + adjective + 了, which covers 太好了, 太贵了 and 太辣了 alike.
太 means both 'so' and 'too much', and the adjective decides which. 太棒了 is praise while 太贵了 (too expensive) and 太辣了 (too spicy) are complaints — same frame, opposite job.
很棒 and 太棒了 do not sit in the same place. 很棒 describes something (this place is great); 太棒了 reacts to something (that's great!). Using 太棒了 as a description is what makes it sound over the top.

when: Only when someone is in real danger — a medical emergency, a fire, a serious accident, or harassment.
Shout it to draw the attention of anyone nearby. It is the one word that reliably stops people in a crowd.

variants.note: A request for help, but nowhere near as urgent as 救命. For being stuck, overloaded or lost rather than in danger.
The everyday request. Perfectly fine when you simply cannot manage on your own.
The follow-up that matters in a medical emergency.

mistakes: 救命 is not 'help me with this bag'. Spending it on a small problem wastes the one word that makes people act — for everything else use 帮忙 or 帮帮我.
Keep it for danger. A bystander who believes you are in danger may well call the police (110) on your behalf, which turns a small problem into a long one.
Emergency numbers in China: 110 police, 120 ambulance, 119 fire. Hotel staff and passers-by can also place the call for you.

replies.en: I'll call an ambulance for you.

when: When something has genuinely gone wrong: a lost passport, a stolen bag, or a phone that has died before you have anywhere to stay.
Say it to staff rather than to a passer-by. Hotel front desks, station service counters and shop assistants can make calls and check records, which strangers cannot.

variants.note: The direct question form. Works well straight after 不好意思 when you are already talking to somebody.
Much lighter, for a small immediate favour such as reading a sign or lifting a bag.

variants.en: I need to see a doctor.
variants.note: The same 我需要 frame carries any need: 我需要充电器 (a charger), 我需要一张地图 (a map).

mistakes: Do not reach for 救命 here. 救命 means somebody's life is in danger, and spending it on a lost phone empties the word for the moment it is really needed.
Name the person you need if you can. 前台 is the hotel front desk and 服务台 is the service counter in a station or a mall, so pointing at it plus 我需要帮助 covers the gap when the sentence runs out.
帮助 is the written and formal word. In speech people say 帮我, which is why 请帮我一下 sounds far more natural at a shop counter.

replies.py: Qǐng shāoděng, wǒ zhǎo gè rén.
replies.en: One moment, let me find someone.

when: You say it when something illegal has happened to you — a theft, a pickpocket, an assault, or a driver who will not settle after an accident.
Say it to hotel staff, a shop assistant or a station attendant rather than to a passer-by: they can place the call and can tell the operator where you are.

variants.note: The number by itself is an instruction, and every adult in China knows it. 一 is read yāo on the phone, so it carries over a noisy line.

variants.en: I want to report a crime.
variants.note: What you say once the call connects, or to a staff member who asks what you need. 报警 is the standard verb for calling the police.

variants.en: I need a copy of the police report.
variants.note: Ask for it before you leave the station. Travel insurers usually want written proof that a report was filed, and it is issued on the spot.

mistakes: 110 is the police, 120 the ambulance and 119 the fire service. Dialling the wrong one is not a disaster because the operators transfer you, but naming the right number gets you there faster.
On the phone 一 is read yāo, not yī. That is why 110 comes out as yāo-yāo-líng and 120 as yāo-èr-líng — and why a number shouted over traffic is still understood.
Police in China take identification from the person reporting. Carry your passport, and for anything involving a hotel room or an insured item keep the registration slip or the receipt with it.

when: A medical emergency where somebody cannot get to hospital on their own.
Say it to whoever is nearest. A clear instruction moves strangers to act far faster than a general cry for help.

variants.note: 快 in front is what makes it urgent. This is the version to shout across a street.
The number alone is an instruction. 120 is the ambulance line and everyone in China knows it.
Explains why you are asking, and gives whoever is listening something to act on.

mistakes: On the phone, 一 is read yāo and not yī. 120 is yāo-èr-líng, which is what makes the number clear over traffic noise.
An ambulance in China is not free: the ride is charged for separately from the hospital bill. Cost should not decide anything in a real emergency, but it is worth knowing this is a paid service.
If the person can walk, a taxi is usually faster. 医院在哪里 plus the nearest driver gets you there sooner than waiting for a crew, and the hospital 急诊 (emergency department) is open all night.

when: Say it while showing someone the Chinese name of your hotel on your phone — names and pictures get you found far faster than any spoken description.
迷路 means to lose your way, and 了 marks the change of state: you were fine a moment ago, and now you are lost.

variants.note: 走丢 is the everyday word for someone who drifted away from their group — also what parents shout about children in a crowd.

variants.en: I want to go back to my hotel.
variants.note: Swap in your hotel's name — 我要回香格里拉 works the same way and names the destination in one go.
Point at the ground under your feet — it makes any local open their map app for you.

mistakes: 迷路 means you yourself are lost; 找不到 means you cannot find something you are looking for. You 迷路 on the street, but you 找不到 your hotel entrance even on a street you know.

Street names in China often change along one road, and building numbers restart at each crossing — directions by address numbers fail fast, so landmarks and shop-front photos beat any verbal description.
For a companion missing in a crowd, use 走丢 too: 我朋友走丢了 (my friend got lost) is understood instantly at any information desk — and loud enough to gather help.

replies.py: Bié jí, wǒ bāng nín kànkan.
replies.en: Don't worry, let me take a look.
Which hotel are you going to?

replies.py: Qiánmiàn lùkǒu yòu zhuǎn jiù dào le.
replies.en: Turn right at the crossing ahead and you are there.

when: When you need care yourself and can still move: a fever that will not break, a sprained ankle, a cut that needs stitches.
Ask a hotel front desk, a pharmacy or a taxi driver. The same question gets you a hospital name, a direction, or a ride.

variants.note: The better question when you have no idea how far it is. 附近 means nearby, and the answer may be a pharmacy instead.
For anything small, start here. Pharmacies are everywhere and the staff will point you to a hospital if the problem is beyond them.
Large Chinese hospitals are several buildings with departments split across them. 急诊 is the one that never closes.

mistakes: The 在哪里 frame takes any place, so learn it once: 药店 pharmacy, 派出所 local police station, 地铁站 metro station, 洗手间 washroom.

Go to a large hospital rather than a small clinic. The biggest hospitals in a city have an international clinic (国际部) used to foreign patients, and 三甲 on the sign is the shorthand for a top-tier hospital.
The emergency department is the right door at night or at a weekend. Registration comes first when you arrive, and the passport is what the desk asks for.

replies.en: Turn right at the junction ahead.

replies.py: Jiù zài zhè tiáo jiē shàng.

when: Say it at a hotel front desk or to anyone nearby when you feel unwell and need medical help rather than a pharmacy.
Chinese hospitals usually take a sudden illness straight into 急诊 (the emergency department), instead of asking you to book a clinic appointment first.

variants.note: 挂号 is the first step of every hospital visit — pay a small fee, get a number, then wait to be called.
A 诊所 handles small problems; a 医院 handles everything else.
The traveler's most common complaint, and the colloquial 拉肚子 is exactly what triage staff expect to hear.

mistakes: The patient 看医生 (sees the doctor) and the doctor 看病 (sees the illness) — the same 看 points both ways, and 我看病 said by a patient is understood as the same thing.
Registering (挂号) is not optional — skip the window and there is no number, and without a number no doctor will call you, however empty the waiting room looks.
A pharmacy (药店) is often the faster stop for minor problems, because pharmacists there recommend and sell medicine directly — more street corners have one than have a clinic.

replies.en: The emergency department is on the first floor.
Go and register over there first.

when: Say it before you order, not after, and name the thing with 对…过敏 — 我过敏 on its own leaves everyone guessing what you need to avoid.
It is the line that gets you a real answer: staff usually know what is in a dish, but the safest version is to show the allergen written in Chinese and confirm it before anything is cooked.

variants.note: Swap in 牛奶 (milk), 鸡蛋 (egg) or 坚果 (nuts) for the same frame. 海鲜 covers fish, prawns, crab and shellfish in one word.

variants.py: Wǒ chī le huì hěn nánshòu.
variants.en: It makes me very ill if I eat it.
variants.note: Some kitchens hear 过敏 as a preference. Saying what happens to you moves it into the safety column, and that is the part that changes how they cook.
The checkable question, and the one worth asking again at the table — 花生油 (peanut oil) is common in Chinese cooking and never appears in a dish name.

mistakes: Allergy is a known idea in China but not a routine one, so 过敏 on its own is often heard as a mild dislike. Adding what happens to you is what turns it into a kitchen instruction.
过敏 needs its target: 我对…过敏 is the frame. 我过敏 by itself is what you say to a doctor, not to someone taking your order.
The riskiest ingredient is the one missing from the name — peanut oil in a stir-fry, sesame paste in a sauce, shrimp paste in a broth. Naming the dish is not enough; name the ingredient.

replies.py: Nà gěi nín huàn yí ge.
replies.en: Then let me swap it for something else.

when: Use it before any dish is chosen — the moment you sit down or open the menu — because peanut oil is common in Chinese kitchens and peanuts hide in dishes that do not look nutty.
过敏 (allergic) is what makes it medical: it is stronger than 我不吃花生 (I don't eat peanuts), which staff will hear as a preference they can talk you out of.

variants.note: 不能 (cannot) beats 不 (don't) here — 不 sounds like a choice, 不能 sounds like a rule, and kitchens take rules more seriously.
Ask it per dish at the same time as you order it — blanket questions about the whole menu get vague answers.
花生油 (peanut oil) is the default frying oil in many kitchens, and 放 is the cooking verb for adding it — this targets the oil, not just whole peanuts.

mistakes: The general allergy phrase 我过敏 (I'm allergic) names no trigger and often gets nothing but a nod. Naming it — 花生, 海鲜 (seafood), 牛奶 (milk), 坚果 (nuts) — is what makes the kitchen act.
Peanuts hide under famous names: 宫保鸡丁 (Kung Pao Chicken) is cooked with peanuts, and so are many cold starters. Ask even for dishes that sound safely meaty.
No visible peanuts is not the same as peanut-free — peanut oil leaves no trace to see. 不放花生油 (no peanut oil) covers the oil, because 没有花生 alone only rules out the nuts themselves.

replies.en: There are some peanuts in it.

when: When you need somebody to understand that you are unwell right now — a hotel front desk, a pharmacy counter, or a colleague you have to cancel on.
Name the symptom straight after it, because 我生病了 on its own says only that something is wrong; 我发烧了 or 我头疼 is what gets a specific answer.

variants.note: The specific one that moves things fastest. A fever is what pharmacies and clinics act on, and it is worth saying before anything else.
Softer and vaguer than 生病了 — 不舒服 covers everything from a headache to an upset stomach without naming it.
我 plus a body part plus 疼 builds any ache: 肚子疼 (stomach), 嗓子疼 (throat), 牙疼 (tooth).

mistakes: Chinese usually names the symptom rather than the general state. The English 'I'm sick' is a complete answer; 我生病了 is a door-opener, and the next question will be 哪里不舒服？ — so have the body part ready.
了 marks a change, so 我生病了 means you were fine and now you are not. For something long-standing you drop it and say 我身体不好, and the two are not interchangeable.

药店 is where you buy medicine and 医院 is where you are treated. Saying 我要去医院 for a headache will be heard as an emergency, so point yourself at 药店 for anything you would fix with over-the-counter medicine.

replies.en: Do you need to go to a hospital?

replies.py: Duō hē rè shuǐ, zǎodiǎn xiūxi.
replies.en: Drink more hot water and get some rest.

when: Use it at any counter when you cannot tell how payment works here — no card reader in sight, no QR code propped up, and nobody has asked you for money yet.
The usual answer is 扫码 (sǎo mǎ, scan the code): either you scan their code with your phone, or they scan the code your app shows, and both directions are called the same thing.

variants.note: For markets and canteens where paying happens at a specific spot — this asks the place rather than the method.
收银台 is the cash register counter in shops and supermarkets — the landmark question when you are standing in the wrong aisle with an armful of goods.

variants.py: Kěyǐ sǎo nín de mǎ ma?
variants.note: Their printed code scanned by your app is one of the two QR directions; asking before pointing your camera keeps the moment friendly.

mistakes: 付款 and 付钱 are the shop verbs; restaurants have their own — 结账 (jiézhàng) or 买单 (mǎidān) is what you say when you want the bill, so in a restaurant the question becomes 怎么结账？

The two QR directions are easy to mix: scanning their code opens a payment page on your phone, while showing your code lets their scanner take money from you. If a staff member grabs your phone, they are doing the second one.
扣款 (kòukuǎn) on a banking app means an automatic deduction — it is not the counter word, and nobody says it when asking you to pay.

when: Say it as the bill arrives and you intend to be the one who pays. Reaching for the QR code while you say it is what makes it land, since the words alone can sound like an offer rather than a decision.
It is also what you say to a friend who is already holding a phone up to the scanner, because 来 means "let me do it" — 我来 claims the action instead of asking permission to do it.

variants.note: 次 counts occasions, so it leaves the next round to the other person.

variants.py: Nǐ lái diǎn, wǒ lái fù.
variants.note: The doubled 来 splits the two jobs neatly, and it settles things before the food even arrives.
转 is the verb for moving money in WeChat or Alipay, and it is the fallback when you are not next to the scanner.

mistakes: 付 is only about handing over money. 我来付 is about the bill, while 我来买 is about buying something, so swapping them turns "I'll pay" into "I'll buy this".
There is no single word that means splitting the bill. 我来付 claims the whole thing; to share it you say 我们 AA (spoken as the two English letters) or 各付各的 (gè fù gè de).
Expect to argue. The other person will say 我来我来 and mean it, and refusing twice before giving in is the script rather than a real conflict.

replies.py: Bù xíng bù xíng, wǒ lái.

when: When you are the one paying for everyone — a meal, a round of drinks, or the shared taxi at the end of the night.
Say it as you sit down or reach for the menu, because the offer to host is a claim you stake early rather than an answer you give when the bill arrives.

variants.note: 顿 is the measure word for meals, so 这顿 pins the treat to this one sitting rather than to a general habit.
算我的 claims the cost without the formal ring of 请客, which is useful when the other person is already reaching for their wallet.

variants.en: Don't stand on ceremony, it's on me.
variants.note: 别客气 is what you say when somebody pushes back. 我请 is 我请客 shortened, which is how it comes out in speech.

mistakes: 请客 is to host, not simply to pay. It carries the idea that you invited them, so announcing it after somebody else picked the restaurant can sound like you are taking over their occasion.

The first offer is usually waved away. Refusing once is the polite move rather than a real no, so 我请客 expects a second or third round before it settles — stopping after one refusal reads as not meaning it.
Do not translate 'split the bill' as 分钱. 分钱 is dividing money in general and can sound like haggling; 各付各的 or AA制 is the phrase for going Dutch.

replies.en: I can't let you do that!
